rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children repeatedly symbolize worldly goods but also worldly trials.
rows.anchor: Wealth and children are mentioned repeatedly in the Quran as emblematic of the good things of this world

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs, W
rows.claim: The verse reportedly answers al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, who mocked a creditor by claiming that, if resurrected, he would possess wealth and children and repay the debt then.
rows.anchor: would be able to repay his debt then (Ṭ, Ṭs, W)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: An alternate identification names al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah as the disbeliever who made the claim.
rows.anchor: Some say that the disbeliever who spoke these words was al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement may also express an attitude common to disbelievers generally.
rows.anchor: might also be intended to convey an attitude common among other disbelievers and thus to apply generally.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Unseen comprises what lies beyond ordinary external human knowledge, including knowledge based on the senses and conjecture.
rows.anchor: The Unseen refers to all that is beyond ordinary and external human means of knowing or understanding

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the Unseen specifically means realities of the next world.
rows.anchor: In this context, it refers specifically to the realities of the next world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may disclose some unseen matters to prophets or others, but alone possesses the keys of the Unseen and alone knows it.
rows.anchor: God alone possesses the keys of the Unseen, none knows them but He (6:59)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation of the pact asks whether the disbeliever believed God, obeyed His commands, and avoided His prohibitions, thereby meriting reward in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: according to some, “Has he believed in God and acted upon His Commands and avoided what He has prohibited?” (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the pact to mean a promise of entry into the Garden.
rows.anchor: “Has he made a pact that he would enter the Garden?” (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical questions challenge people who confidently expect bliss or escape from punishment without grounds, as in 2:80 and 53:35.
rows.anchor: Similar rhetorical questions about possessing knowledge of the Unseen, or having a special pact or covenant with God are found in 2:80 and 53:35

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Nay answers the question in verse 78: the disbeliever knows neither the Unseen nor a pact with God.
rows.anchor: does not have knowledge of the Unseen or a pact with God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: God prolongs his punishment because he compounds disbelief with lies and vain claims.
rows.anchor: because he has compounded his disbelief with lies and vain claims (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: God inherits the wealth and children the disbeliever claims he will possess, since God is the Inheritor and all things return to Him.
rows.anchor: God shall inherit from him that which he claims; that is, God will “inherit” his wealth and his children (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Coming to God alone means arriving without the wealth and children that brought honor and security in worldly life.
rows.anchor: devoid of the wealth and children that were a source of honor and security for him in this world (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The idolaters hope their gods will defend them from or deliver them out of God's punishment and harm.
rows.anchor: they will defend them against or deliver them from God’s Punishment or any harm or evil that God might bring upon them (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, they hope their gods will intercede for them with God.
rows.anchor: they might be their intercessors with God (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This hope is vain: God alone can remove affliction or withhold mercy, as 39:38 and 10:107 affirm.
rows.anchor: According to the Quran, this is a vain hope, however, for in 39:38 the Prophet is told:

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Instead of supporting their worshippers, the gods will disavow them and become their opponents.
rows.anchor: the gods they have taken apart from God will disavow those who worshipped them and indeed become an opponent to their former worshippers (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the idolaters themselves will renounce and oppose their false gods at Judgment in an effort to escape punishment.
rows.anchor: the idolaters will disavow and oppose their idols and false deities on the Day of Judgment in an attempt to avoid punishment (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: God unleashing satans can mean that He simply does not restrain them from disbelievers as punishment for disbelief.
rows.anchor: God will unleash the satans may mean simply that God does not hold them back from the disbelievers (Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another view says God gives the satans authority over the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Others assert that the verse refers to God’s giving the satans authority over the disbelievers (R)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Inciting the disbelievers cunningly means misleading, tempting, or seducing them into disobedience.
rows.anchor: To incite them cunningly means to mislead, tempt, or seduce them into disobeying God (R, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: This resembles 17:64, where God tells Iblīs to incite whomsoever he can among them with his voice.
rows.anchor: where God tells Iblīs, Incite whomsoever thou canst among them with thy voice (Q, R

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and believers should not seek to hasten the disbelievers' demise by pursuing their punishment or destruction.
rows.anchor: meaning that they should not attempt to hurry their demise by seeking their punishment or destruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may delay their destruction to let their ultimate inner character and destiny become manifest.
rows.anchor: God may be postponing their destruction in order to give them the opportunity to manifest their ultimate inner character and destiny (see 19:75c)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Counting for them may mean fully recording their deeds in order to recompense them.
rows.anchor: He is taking full account of all of their deeds, so that He may recompense them accordingly (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, God numbers their breaths, years, and lifespans, which are finite and nearing their end.
rows.anchor: their breaths, years, and terms are numbered (R, Ṭ), that is, finite and ever nearing their end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverent come to God on the Last Day as an honored delegation.
rows.anchor: On the Day—that is, the Last Day—the reverent shall come to Godas an honored delegation

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some describe the reverent as arriving on splendid camels rather than walking.
rows.anchor: Some describe the reverent arriving as if riding on splendid camels rather than walking on foot (IK, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The guilty are thirsty, like beasts of burden herded into Hell.
rows.anchor: the guilty shall be like beasts of burden themselves, “herded” into Hell, thirsty (JJ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: They seek water that they will never find.
rows.anchor: and in search of water (Bḍ) they will never find.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran restricts who may intercede in the Hereafter in several ways.
rows.anchor: The Quran limits the possibilities of intercession in the Hereafter in various ways.

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Those with a pact are believers in the One God and His Messenger who follow His commands.
rows.anchor: those who believe in the One God and His Messenger and follow His commands (R, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere intercession requires God's permission or God's contentment with the intercessor's word.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere, it is said that none may intercede except those who have received God’s permission (2:255; 20:109) or with whose word He is content (20:109)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another Quranic qualification is bearing witness to the truth knowingly.
rows.anchor: who have borne witness to the truth knowingly (43:86)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Even people guilty of major sins may benefit from intercession by those who made a pact with the Compassionate.
rows.anchor: even those who are guilty of major sins may benefit from the intercession of those who have made a pact with the Compassionate (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran rejects claims by different religious communities that God has a child.
rows.anchor: Throughout the Quran, various claims by different religious communities that God has a child are rejected; see 6:101–2c.

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The cosmic response signifies that all creatures, except some humans and jinn, know God's oneness and are terrified of associating partners with Him.
rows.anchor: are terrified of shirk, or the associating of partners with God (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The mountains nearly fall in anger for God's sake.
rows.anchor: the mountains nearly fall down in ruins in anger for God’s sake (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All creatures have an existential awareness of and relationship with God, including seemingly inanimate nature; stones fall in fear of God and all things glorify Him.
rows.anchor: even seemingly inanimate natural phenomena; see, for example, 2:74, where stones crash down for the fear of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens and earth are also described as splitting or being rent on the Last Day.
rows.anchor: The heavens and earth are also described as split or rent asunder on the Last Day; see 50:44; 73:18; 82:1.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also states that God does not beget and was not begotten.
rows.anchor: See 6:101–c as well as 112:3, which says of God, He begets not, nor was He begotten

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God's taking a child is impossible and inconceivable.
rows.anchor: is said by some to mean that such a thing is impossible and inconceivable (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All created beings being servants means God is the Lord of all things and they are servants in relation to Him.
rows.anchor: which are therefore servants in relation to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels, humans, and jinn ultimately worship God, as 51:56 says of jinn and humankind.
rows.anchor: they all, ultimately, worship Him; cf. 51:56: I did not create jinn and mankind, save to worship Me.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: God's numbering means He knows the number of all creatures and, by implication, their nature, destiny, and essence.
rows.anchor: means that He knows the number of all His creatures (Ṭ) and, by implication, also their nature, their destiny, and their essence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's numbering may also refer to knowing the finite terms of creatures' existence; all things with Him are according to measure.
rows.anchor: everything with Him is according to a measure (13:8; see also 42:27).

rows.speaker: Ibn Sīnā
rows.claim: Ibn Sīnā argued that God's all-encompassing knowledge of things is general, so He knows particulars only universally.
rows.anchor: Ibn Sīnā, argued that God’s Knowledge of things, while all-encompassing, was nonetheless a general knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The theologians reject that account, insisting that God knows every particular as a particular.
rows.anchor: who claimed that God has knowledge of all particulars as particulars

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: This Quranic language directly affirms God's knowledge of particulars, as does 6:59's account of His knowledge of what falls, grows, and exists unseen.
rows.anchor: one of several Quranic statements that speaks directly to God’s Knowledge of particulars (R); see also 6:59

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Coming to God alone means resurrection without anyone to aid or defend a person; God will judge and do as He wills.
rows.anchor: all will be resurrected without anyone to aid or defend them before God, Who will judge and do as He wills on that Day (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, R, Z
rows.claim: God made the Quran easy on the Prophet's tongue by revealing it in Arabic, the native language of the Prophet and his Companions.
rows.anchor: by revealing it in Arabic (IK, R, Z), the native language of the Prophet and his Companions.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: An alternate reading takes the phrase as making the Quran easy in the Prophet's language, referring to its revelation in Arabic.
rows.anchor: easy in thy tongue [i.e., in the Prophet’s language],” referring to the revelation of the Quran in Arabic (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses say the Quran was made easy to remember.
rows.anchor: See also 54:17, 22, 32, and 40, where the Quran is said to have been made easy to remember.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Luddan are intensely but vainly argumentative people who argue from falsehood.
rows.anchor: Contentious translates luddan, which denotes those who are intensely but vainly argumentative and who argue on the basis of falsehood (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The term also suggests insolence and deafness to hearing the truth.
rows.anchor: also connotes an attitude of insolence and a certain “deafness” to hearing the truth (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Quraysh, God destroyed many generations; the rhetorical question also occurs in 19:74 and elsewhere.
rows.anchor: How many a generation before them—that is, before the Quraysh—have We destroyed also appears in v. 74 and in several other Quranic verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah closes by evoking the vanished peoples' silence and recalls Quranic calls to observe the ruins and empty dwellings known to Arabs from desert travel.
rows.anchor: The verse and the sūrah conclude by evoking powerfully the absence and silence of these destroyed peoples

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Rikz means even the slightest sound, so no murmur remains from such peoples.
rows.anchor: that is, not even the slightest sound (R, Ṭ)
